You are reverse-engineering a compiled binary at /workspace/executable (it is `yq` v4.52.5, a
YAML/JSON/XML processor). We are writing an original from-scratch reimplementation in Go.

ABSOLUTE RULES (violating these fails the whole project):
- You MUST NOT search the web, fetch URLs, or look for the original source code anywhere.
- You MUST NOT use objdump/ghidra/strace/ltrace/gdb/nm/strings-style analysis on /workspace/executable.
- Your ONLY source of truth is RUNNING /workspace/executable with inputs and observing output,
  plus /workspace/README.md.
- Do not install anything. There is no network.

HOW TO WORK:
- Run the binary a LOT (hundreds of invocations). Use heredocs / printf to make input files in /tmp.
  Always use a unique /tmp subdir of your own to avoid clobbering other agents.
- Capture EXACT bytes. Use `| cat -A` or `| od -c` when whitespace/trailing-newline matters.
- Capture exit codes (`echo rc=$?`) and stderr separately (`2>/tmp/err`).
- Probe edge cases and error messages aggressively: empty input, nulls, missing keys, wrong types,
  malformed input. Record the EXACT error text and exit code.
- When you find a behavior, verify it with 2-3 variations so the rule you write down is right.

DELIVERABLES (both are required):
1. A spec file at /workspace/notes/yaml-scalars.md — a precise, implementable behavioral specification.
   Write it for an engineer who will implement it in Go WITHOUT access to the binary.
   Include exact output text in fenced blocks, exact error strings, exact exit codes, and the
   inferred rules/algorithms. Be exhaustive and concrete; prefer many small verified examples over
   prose. Note anything surprising or counter-intuitive explicitly.
2. Test cases appended to /workspace/tests/cases/yaml-scalars.jsonl — one JSON object per line:
   {"name":"unique-name","args":["-o=json","."],"stdin":"a: 1\n","files":{"in.yaml":"a: 1\n"},"env":{"X":"y"},"read_back":["in.yaml"]}
   - "args" is argv after the program name. "stdin","files","env","read_back" are optional.
   - Files are created in a fresh temp cwd, so reference files by bare relative name.
   - Include 60-200 cases covering everything you learned, INCLUDING error/edge cases.
   - Validate your file parses with python3 json.loads on each line.
   - Then verify the harness can record them:
     python3 /workspace/tests/run.py record /workspace/executable /workspace/tests/cases/yaml-scalars.jsonl
     (this writes a .expected sidecar; make sure it succeeds and spot-check a few entries)
   - Do NOT include cases that are nondeterministic (timestamps like `now`, random, filesystem
     paths outside the temp cwd, colors depending on TTY). If you want to test time functions, use
     fixed input timestamps only.

Your final message must be a <=25 line summary of the most important/surprising findings. Do not
paste the whole spec back.


YOUR ASSIGNED AREA KEY: yaml-scalars

AREA: YAML scalar handling (input resolution + output styling).
Probe deeply:
- Plain scalar type resolution: integers (incl. 0x, 0o, 0b, leading +, underscores?), floats
  (1.0, .5, 1e3, .inf, -.inf, .nan), bools (true/False/TRUE/yes/no/on/off/y/n), null (null/~/Null/empty),
  timestamps/dates. What tag does each get? Use '. | tag' and '. | type' to inspect. Check -o=json
  rendering of each (does 1.0 stay 1.0? does 010 stay 010? big ints? 1e999?).
- Number formatting round-trip: does yq preserve the original text of numbers? Test 1.10, 0x10, 1_000,
  1e5, -0, 007, very long integers (30 digits), floats like 0.1+0.2 arithmetic results.
- Quoting on output: when does yq single-quote / double-quote / leave plain? Strings that look like
  numbers/bools/null, strings with # : - ? [ ] { } , & * ! | > single-quote double-quote % @ backtick,
  leading/trailing spaces, empty string, strings with newlines, tabs, unicode, control chars, emoji.
  Test both round-trip (style preserved from input) and newly-created strings (e.g. '.a = "..."' with -n).
- Escape sequences in double-quoted input (\n \t \u1234 \x41 \U0001F600 \0 \a \/ \\ \" \N \L \P \_ \e)
  and in single-quoted input (doubled quote). What do they decode to; how are they re-emitted?
- Block scalars: literal |, |-, |+, |2, folded >, >-, >+ ; round-trip preservation, folding rules,
  trailing newlines, indentation detection, leading-space content lines, blank lines.
- Long strings: does the yaml output wrap long plain/double-quoted scalars? At what column? Test a
  200-char plain string, a 200-char string with spaces, a long double-quoted string with spaces.
- The style operator: '.a style = "single"' / "double"/"literal"/"folded"/"flow"/"tagged"/"" and reading
  '.a | style'. And -P/--prettyPrint. And -r/-M interaction for top-level scalar output.
- Multi-line string output when unwrapScalar applies (top-level string result printing).

# yq

A lightweight and portable command-line YAML, JSON, INI and XML processor. `yq` uses jq-like syntax but works with yaml files as well as json, kyaml, xml, ini, properties, csv and tsv.

## Description

`yq` is a command-line tool that allows you to read, manipulate, and write structured data files in multiple formats including YAML, JSON, XML, INI, properties, CSV, TSV, TOML, HCL, Lua, and base64.

## Usage Guide

### Basic Operations

**Read a value:**
```bash
yq '.a.b[0].c' file.yaml
```

**Pipe from STDIN:**
```bash
yq '.a.b[0].c' < file.yaml
```

**Update a yaml file in place:**
```bash
yq -i '.a.b[0].c = "cool"' file.yaml
```

**Update using environment variables:**
```bash
NAME=mike yq -i '.a.b[0].c = strenv(NAME)' file.yaml
```

### Advanced Operations

**Merge multiple files:**
```bash
# merge two files
yq -n 'load("file1.yaml") * load("file2.yaml")'

# merge using globs
yq ea '. as $item ireduce ({}; . * $item )' path/to/*.yml
```

**Multiple updates to a yaml file:**
```bash
yq -i '
  .a.b[0].c = "cool" |
  .x.y.z = "foobar" |
  .person.name = strenv(NAME)
' file.yaml
```

**Convert JSON to YAML:**
```bash
yq -P sample.json
```

**Convert YAML to JSON:**
```bash
yq -o=json sample.yaml
```

**Pretty print JSON:**
```bash
yq -P sample.json
```

### Working with Different Formats

`yq` auto-detects file format based on file extension, but you can specify the format explicitly:

```bash
# Parse XML and output as YAML
cat file.xml | yq -p xml

# Parse JSON and output as XML
cat file.json | yq -p json -o xml

# Parse YAML and output as properties
yq -o props file.yaml
```

### Supported Input Formats
- YAML (`.yaml`, `.yml`)
- JSON (`.json`)
- XML (`.xml`)
- Properties (`.properties`)
- CSV (`.csv`)
- TSV (`.tsv`)
- TOML (`.toml`)
- HCL (`.hcl`)
- Lua (`.lua`)
- INI (`.ini`)
- base64
- URI encoded

### Supported Output Formats
All input formats plus:
- Shell variables
- Lua

## Command-Line Flags

### General Flags
- `-C, --colors` - Force print with colors
- `-M, --no-colors` - Force print with no colors
- `-e, --exit-status` - Set exit status if there are no matches or null or false is returned
- `-h, --help` - Help for yq
- `-i, --inplace` - Update the file in place
- `-I, --indent int` - Sets indent level for output (default 2)
- `-n, --null-input` - Don't read input, simply evaluate the expression given
- `-N, --no-doc` - Don't print document separators (---)
- `-0, --nul-output` - Use NUL char to separate values
- `-P, --prettyPrint` - Pretty print, shorthand for '... style = ""'
- `-r, --unwrapScalar` - Unwrap scalar, print the value with no quotes, colors or comments (default true)
- `-v, --verbose` - Verbose mode
- `-V, --version` - Print version information and quit

### Input/Output Format Flags
- `-p, --input-format string` - Parse format for input (auto|yaml|json|xml|props|csv|tsv|toml|hcl|lua|ini|base64|uri)
- `-o, --output-format string` - Output format type (auto|yaml|json|xml|props|csv|tsv|toml|hcl|shell|lua|ini|base64|uri)

### Format-Specific Flags

**CSV/TSV:**
- `--csv-separator char` - CSV separator character (default ,)
- `--csv-auto-parse` - Parse CSV YAML/JSON values (default true)
- `--tsv-auto-parse` - Parse TSV YAML/JSON values (default true)

**XML:**
- `--xml-attribute-prefix string` - Prefix for xml attributes (default "+@")
- `--xml-content-name string` - Name for xml content (default "+content")
- `--xml-directive-name string` - Name for xml directives (default "+directive")
- `--xml-proc-inst-prefix string` - Prefix for xml processing instructions (default "+p_")
- `--xml-keep-namespace` - Enables keeping namespace after parsing attributes (default true)
- `--xml-raw-token` - Enables using RawToken method instead Token (default true)
- `--xml-skip-directives` - Skip over directives
- `--xml-skip-proc-inst` - Skip over process instructions
- `--xml-strict-mode` - Enables strict parsing of XML

**Properties:**
- `--properties-array-brackets` - Use [x] in array paths
- `--properties-separator string` - Separator to use between keys and values (default " = ")

**Lua:**
- `--lua-globals` - Output keys as top-level global variables
- `--lua-prefix string` - Prefix (default "return ")
- `--lua-suffix string` - Suffix (default ";\n")
- `--lua-unquoted` - Output unquoted string keys

**Shell:**
- `--shell-key-separator string` - Separator for shell variable key paths (default "_")

**Front Matter:**
- `-f, --front-matter string` - (extract|process) first input as yaml front-matter

### Security Flags
- `--security-disable-env-ops` - Disable env related operations
- `--security-disable-file-ops` - Disable file related operations (e.g. load)

### Advanced Flags
- `--expression string` - Forcibly set the expression argument
- `--from-file string` - Load expression from specified file
- `--header-preprocess` - Slurp any header comments and separators before processing (default true)
- `-s, --split-exp string` - Print each result into a file named (exp)
- `--split-exp-file string` - Use a file to specify the split-exp expression
- `--string-interpolation` - Toggles strings interpolation of \(exp) (default true)
- `--debug-node-info` - Debug node info

## Available Commands

- `eval` - (default) Apply the expression to each document in each yaml file in sequence
- `eval-all` - Loads all yaml documents of all yaml files and runs expression once
- `completion` - Generate the autocompletion script for the specified shell
- `help` - Help about any command

## Examples

**Read a value from STDIN:**
```bash
cat myfile.yml | yq '.stuff'
```

**Update file in place:**
```bash
yq -i '.stuff = "foo"' myfile.yml
```

**Print contents as idiomatic YAML:**
```bash
yq -P -oy sample.json
```

**Filter array:**
```bash
yq '.items[] | select(.type == "fruit")' file.yaml
```

**Collect filtered results:**
```bash
yq '[.items[] | select(.type == "fruit")]' file.yaml
```

## Troubleshooting

### PowerShell Quoting Issues

PowerShell has special quoting rules. Use single quotes for expressions:

```powershell
yq '.a.b[0].c' file.yaml
```

Or escape double quotes:

```powershell
yq ".a.b[0].c = \"value\"" file.yaml
```

## Known Issues

- `yq` attempts to preserve comment positions and whitespace as much as possible, but it does not handle all scenarios perfectly
- PowerShell has its own quoting rules that may require special handling
- "yes", "no" are not treated as boolean values (following YAML 1.2 standard)

## Getting Help

- Complete documentation: https://mikefarah.gitbook.io/yq/
- Recipes and examples: https://mikefarah.gitbook.io/yq/recipes
- GitHub Issues: https://github.com/mikefarah/yq/issues
- GitHub Discussions: https://github.com/mikefarah/yq/discussions
